title: Doubt
hookLine: doubt is not unbelief; Thomas doubted and was still an apostle

cards: Thomas missed the meeting. On the evening the tomb is found empty, the disciples are behind locked doors, and the risen Jesus stands among them. Thomas isn't there.
When he gets back, the others are almost shouting: we have seen the Lord. And Thomas says no.

"Except I shall see in his hands the print of the nails, and put my finger into the print of the nails, and thrust my hand into his side, I will not believe." For a whole week he's the one in the room who can't say yes.

teach.b: You met Thomas in year one; today, a closer look. After eight days the doors are shut again, and this time Thomas is there. Jesus goes straight to him.

No scolding speech. He offers exactly what Thomas asked for: "Reach hither thy finger, and behold my hands; and reach hither thy hand, and thrust it into my side: and be not faithless, but believing."
The doubter gets a visit of his own. Then what Thomas says. The text never says he touched the wounds.
He answers, "My Lord and my God." The man remembered for doubting calls Jesus, plainly, both Lord and God. The doubt didn't disqualify him; it was the road he took to get there.
At the end of Matthew's Gospel, the disciples meet Jesus on a mountain: "they worshipped him: but some doubted." Worship and doubt in one sentence, one crowd, and Jesus sends all of them out anyway.
In Mark, a desperate father brings his son to Jesus and cries out, "Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief." Both in one breath, and Jesus heals the boy. Last, where Thomas went.

teach.h: TRADITION SAYS: ALL THE WAY TO INDIA.
teach.b: Tradition says he traveled east, as far as India, and some Christians in India keep that story as their own. The doubter, in that telling, became a messenger to a far country. So some Christians draw a line here.
Unbelief walks away. Doubt stays in the room and asks to see.

how: Christians remember Thomas on his feast day and read his story in church on the Sunday after Easter in some traditions; some churches hold groups where questions and doubts are spoken aloud, and the father's prayer from Mark is prayed as a short prayer of its own.

games.q: you're Thomas. your friends swear they've seen Jesus alive, and you weren't there. what do you say?
o: unless I see the nails and touch his side, I won't believe.
games.why: Thomas asks to see for himself. he stays with the others for a week, still unsure, and Jesus comes back for him.

practice: Let one honest question come up, about God, about faith, about a story you've heard, or about yourself, and name it in one plain sentence, the way Thomas did: here's what I can't say yes to yet.
Don't argue with it or rush to answer it; breathe beside it, the way you'd sit beside a friend who's unsure. If you pray, you can borrow the father's words: Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief.

wordCard.voice: Doubt. An honest question that stays in the room. Thomas doubted, was visited, and spoke the words my Lord and my God.

orig.note: Greek: faithless, unbelieving, in "be not faithless, but believing." the opposite is πιστός, believing.

carryVoice: Your line: doubt belongs. Thomas was visited, not sent away. See you in the morning.
